Offspring
OFF-spring
n.
From off plus spring, that which springs from. Webster 1828: a child or children; a descendant or descendants, however remote from the stock; and, figuratively, production of any kind. The Authorized Version uses it of a man’s posterity, of the human race as God’s creation, and once of Christ Himself.

Biblical Definition

Offspring in the Old Testament is a man’s posterity, and it is normally paired with seed. Eliphaz promises Job, thy seed shall be great, and thine offspring as the grass of the earth (Job 5:25), and Job later observes the wicked whose seed is established in their sight with them, and their offspring before their eyes (Job 21:8). Isaiah makes it the object of covenant promise: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring (Isaiah 44:3), and their seed shall be known among the Gentiles, and their offspring among the people: all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed which the LORD hath blessed (Isaiah 61:9). In the New Testament Paul stands on Mars’ hill and quotes a Greek poet back at the Athenians: as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring (Acts 17:28), and draws the conclusion at once: Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device (Acts 17:29). The last use is the Lord’s own: I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star (Revelation 22:16) — David’s descendant and David’s origin at once.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines OFFSPRING as a child or children; a descendant or descendants, however remote from the stock; and, figuratively, production of any kind. The word is native English for what Scripture usually calls seed.

expand to see more

OFFSPRING, n. — A child or children; a descendant or descendants, however remote from the stock.

Production of any kind; as, the offspring of the brain.

The word is a compound of off and spring — that which springs off from a stock — and it carries the same botanical picture as the biblical seed, branch, and root.

Key Scripture

Job 5:25 — "Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be great, and thine offspring as the grass of the earth."

Isaiah 44:3 — "For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring:"

Isaiah 61:9 — "And their seed shall be known among the Gentiles, and their offspring among the people: all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed which the LORD hath blessed."

Acts 17:29 — "Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device."

Revelation 22:16 — "I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star."

Modern Corruption

Acts 17:28 is corrupted when Paul’s we are also his offspring is made a doctrine of universal spiritual sonship — every person a child of God in the saving sense — which is precisely the opposite of the argument Paul builds on it.

expand to see more

Paul quotes the poet Aratus to establish creaturely dependence, not saving sonship, and the very next sentence shows what he is doing with it: since we are God’s offspring, we must not imagine the Godhead is like gold or silver graven by art. The argument is against idolatry, and it ends with a command: God… now commandeth all men every where to repent: because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:30-31). The universal fatherhood of God in the liberal sense — all men saved sons, needing only to realize it — takes Paul’s premise and deletes his conclusion. John draws the distinction the New Testament actually teaches: as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name (John 1:12). All men are God’s creatures and image-bearers; not all are His sons by adoption.

The positive doctrine in the word is worth keeping, because it grounds human dignity where Scripture grounds it. Every human being is God’s offspring by creation, which is why murder is an assault on God’s image (Genesis 9:6) and why Athens’ idols were an insult to the Athenians as well as to God. And Revelation 22:16 keeps the deepest paradox in the word: Christ is at once the root and the offspring of David — the source from which David sprang and the descendant who sprang from him. That is the mystery our Lord pressed on the Pharisees from Psalm 110, and it is why the genealogies and the eternal generation of the Son must be held together.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew is usually tse'etsa', that which comes forth, paired with zera', seed; the Greek is genos, kind or race, in Acts 17 and the botanical genos again in Revelation 22:16.

expand to see more

Hebrew tse'etsa' (H6631) — that which issues, offspring, produce; Job 5:25, Isaiah 44:3, Isaiah 61:9.

Hebrew zera' (H2233) — seed; the constant partner of tse'etsa', and the word of the protevangelium in Genesis 3:15.

Greek genos (G1085) — kind, race, stock, offspring; we are also his offspring (Acts 17:28-29) and the offspring of David (Revelation 22:16).

Greek rhiza (G4491) — root; the paired title in Revelation 22:16 and the root of Jesse of Isaiah 11:10.

The pairing of root and offspring in one title asserts both the eternal deity of the Son and His true descent from David according to the flesh.

Usage

"I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring (Isaiah 44:3) — covenant blessing reaching the generations."

"Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God (Acts 17:29) — creaturely dependence used as an argument against idols, not for universal sonship."

"I am the root and the offspring of David (Revelation 22:16) — David’s source and David’s descendant in one Person."
